identification.summary: Amethyst Rain is Microsoft's name for a Lebanon-origin espionage cluster that other vendors track as Volatile Cedar (Check Point), Lebanese Cedar (ClearSky) and DeftTorero (Kaspersky); Microsoft's mapping lists VolcanicTimber and Volatile Cedar as other-vendor names [S1][S2]. Check Point first publicly documented the campaign in 2015, dating it to late 2012 [S3][S4]. Its signature is initial access through vulnerable public-facing web servers rather than phishing, followed by web shells and the custom Explosive RAT [S3][S5][S7].
identification.notes: Microsoft's Rain family name maps to Lebanon-origin actors [S2]. Kaspersky states the group was publicly disclosed as early as 2015 and describes intrusions from late 2019 to mid-2021 [S7][S8]. Name overlap with ClearSky's Lebanese Cedar and Kaspersky's DeftTorero is stated by those sources' own coverage; Microsoft's own reporting on the cluster was not located [S5][S7]. Do not merge Microsoft's POLONIUM/Plaid Rain (also Lebanon-linked) with this cluster [S2].

attribution.sponsor: Not established by Microsoft in sources reviewed. Check Point suspected a Lebanese origin; ClearSky reported indications linking the group to the Hezbollah Cyber Unit [S3][S5][S6].
attribution.confidence: Low to moderate. Check Point said attribution is tricky and deception-prone [S3]; ClearSky language is 'several indications' [S5]; Kaspersky says only 'suspected to originate from Lebanon' [S7]. No government attribution located.
attribution.basis: Check Point noted the victim set aligned with nation-state or political-group interests and suspected Lebanon [S4][S3]. ClearSky cited Check Point's assessment of a link to the Lebanese government or a Lebanese political group and said indications point to the Hezbollah Cyber Unit (as reported by secondary coverage) [S5][S6]. Kaspersky repeats the suspected Lebanon origin [S7].

objectives: Intelligence collection and data theft from government, military, defense, telecom, media and education targets, per vendor characterizations of the campaign as cyber espionage [S3][S4][S5][S7]. ClearSky reported database theft from compromised servers [S5].

targeting.notes: Check Point (2015) reported infections in at least 10 countries incl. US, UK, Israel and Turkey across defense, telecom, media and education [S3][S4]. ClearSky (2021) reported about 250 compromised public-facing web servers since early 2020, a partial list, at telecoms/ISPs in the US, UK, Egypt, Israel, Lebanon, Jordan, Palestinian Authority, Saudi Arabia and UAE [S5][S6]. Kaspersky (2022) lists government, military, education, corporate and telecom targets in UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Kuwait, Lebanon, Jordan and Turkey [S7].

capabilities.summary: Initial access is via internet-exposed web servers instead of spear phishing or drive-by downloads [S3]. The 2015 campaign used the custom Explosive RAT, with USB-based spread and manual lateral movement; the implant limited memory use and observed 'radio silence' periods to evade detection [S3][S4]. In 2020-21 ClearSky observed exploitation of Atlassian Confluence (CVE-2019-3396), Atlassian Jira (CVE-2019-11581) and Oracle 10g (CVE-2012-3152), with a modified JSP file browser, Caterpillar web shell and new Explosive versions [S5][S6]. Kaspersky observed intrusions (late 2019 to mid-2021) beginning with web-server compromise via a file upload form or command injection, web shells, credential reuse, and a possible shift to fileless techniques; a third-party summary of its report lists Mimikatz, Mimikittenz, Empire loader, Meterpreter, PowerSploit, Regeorg and ASPXSpy [S7][S8].

campaigns.name: Volatile Cedar / Explosive campaign begins
campaigns.summary: Check Point dated the campaign to late 2012 [S3][S4].

campaigns.name: Check Point public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Check Point named Volatile Cedar, reporting web-server entry points, Explosive RAT, victims in defense, telecom, media and education in at least 10 countries, and a suspected Lebanese origin [S3][S4].

campaigns.name: Web server mass compromise (ClearSky report, 2021-01)
campaigns.summary: ClearSky reported about 250 public-facing servers hacked since early 2020 via Atlassian and Oracle flaws, with web shells and Explosive RAT, targeting telcos and ISPs [S5][S6].

campaigns.name: DeftTorero intrusions (Kaspersky report, 2022-10)
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky described intrusions from late 2019 to mid-2021 that began with web-server compromise and webshell deployment, followed by internal tool deployment, with a possible shift to fileless techniques [S7][S8].

diamond.adversary: Lebanon-origin espionage cluster; possible Hezbollah Cyber Unit link per ClearSky, not confirmed [S5][S7].
diamond.capability: Explosive RAT, Caterpillar and other web shells, JSP file browser, credential tools, exploitation of known web-app CVEs [S3][S5][S7][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised public-facing web servers used as entry points and footholds [S3][S5]. C2 details not sourced.
diamond.victim: Defense, telecom/ISP, media, education, government and military organizations, concentrated in the Middle East with US/UK reach [S3][S5][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Victim set aligned with regional political and national-security interests, per Check Point and ClearSky [S4][S5].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing web servers (Atlassian Confluence/Jira, Oracle, web upload forms) and internal Windows/web environments [S5][S7].

gaps: Microsoft's own report on Amethyst Rain was not found; naming rests on its mapping file and secondary coverage [S1][S2].
Primary Check Point, ClearSky and Securelist documents could not be fetched (host unreachable); details rely on search summaries and press coverage.
Sponsor and Hezbollah link unconfirmed; no government attribution located.
IOCs, C2 infrastructure and Microsoft-observed TTPs not sourced.
VolcanicTimber origin and vendor not identified in sources reviewed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: the operational environment includes internet-facing web servers at telecom/ISP, defense, media and education organizations, particularly in the Middle East [S5][S7]. Step 3: the actor's observed entry vector is exploitation of unpatched public web applications followed by web shells and RAT/credential tooling [S3][S5][S7]. MLCOA: continued opportunistic web-server compromise for collection against regional telecoms and government (inference from S5, S7). MDCOA: use of compromised telecom/ISP servers as a springboard for downstream customers (inference). Candidate indicators: new web shells (Caterpillar, ASPXSpy) or JSP file browsers on Atlassian/Oracle hosts, Regeorg tunnelling, Mimikatz use on web servers [S5][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: prioritize monitoring of exposed web-application tiers and partner/host-nation telecom links given reported targeting [S5][S7]. Authorities: host-nation and commercial network owners control remediation; coordinate through established DCO/CSSP channels. Mission assurance: patch or isolate internet-facing Atlassian/Oracle systems and inspect for web shells on mission-supporting hosts [S5]. Coordination: share indicators with vendors and partners; treat attribution as unconfirmed [S5][S7].
